q: 1. A simply supported beam which carries a uniformly distributed load has two equal overhangs. To have maximum B.M. produced in the beam least possible, the ratio of length of the overhang to the total length of the beam is
explain: For a beam with equal overhangs under UDL, equating the numerically equal midspan sagging moment and overhang hogging moment gives an optimum overhang ratio of approximately 0.207 (i.e., 0.5(√2 − 1) of the span between supports).

q: 2. The point of contraflexure is the point where
explain: By definition, the point of contraflexure is where the bending moment diagram crosses zero, i.e. where the bending moment changes sign from sagging to hogging or vice versa.

q: 3. A simply supported uniform rectangular bar breadth b, depth d and length L, carries an isolated load W at its mid span. The same bar experiences an extension e under same tensile load. The ratio of the maximum deflection to the elongation is
explain: Comparing the standard bending deflection formula (WL³/48EI) to the axial elongation formula (WL/AE) for the same bar and load leads to a ratio proportional to (L/2d)², as given in option (c); note options c and d are printed identically in the source book.

q: 4. Along the neutral axis of a simply supported beam
explain: By definition, the neutral axis is the layer where bending stress and strain are zero.

q: 5. A simply supported beam carries a varying load from zero at one end to w at the other end. If the length of the beam is a, the shear force will be zero at a distance x from least loaded point where x is
explain: For a triangularly (linearly) varying load, the shear force becomes zero at x = a/√3 measured from the zero-load end, a standard result for such loading.

q: 6. The algebraic sum of the vertical forces on either side of the section of a loaded beam is known as
explain: Shear force at any section is the net vertical force acting on one side of that section.

q: 7. Find the shear force produced in the member BC due to load shown in fig.
explain: Based on the figure, the vertical load applied at C is 4 kN, which remains constant through the member BC.

q: 8. The algebraic sum of the moments of the forces on either side of the section of a loaded beam is known as
explain: This is the formal definition of the internal bending moment at a specific point in a beam.

q: 9. The shear force on a beam and the displacement are related by
explain: Bending Moment M = EI(d²y/dx²). Since V = dM/dx, it follows that V = EI(d³y/dx³).

q: 10. Calculate the maximum BM introduced due to a udl of 4KN/m, if the span of the cantilever is 1.8m
explain: Maximum BM for a cantilever with UDL is wL²/2. (4 × 1.8²) / 2 = 6.48 KN-M.

q: 11. The difference in placing the end of a beam simply over a support and the supporting end through a hinge on rollers is that the roller support
options: can offer reaction in the plane of rollers
will not allowed the end to lift up the deflection
will not offer reaction normal to the plane of rollers
explain: A roller support allows horizontal movement and rotation but constrains vertical movement; however, in standard civil engineering contexts, it prevents the beam from lifting off the support surface.

q: 12. Bending moment at any section in a conjugate beam gives in the actual beam
explain: By the conjugate beam method, the bending moment computed on the conjugate beam at any section corresponds to the deflection at that section in the real (actual) beam.

q: 13. A simply supported beam of span L carries two equal concentrated loads, W at a distance of L/3 from either support. The maximum bending moment, M is
explain: The reaction at each support is W. The maximum moment occurs between the two loads and is equal to Reaction × Distance = W × (L/3).

q: 14. If the width b and depth d of a beam simply supported with a central load are interchanged, the deflection at the centre of the beam will be changed in the ratio of
explain: Since I ∝ bd³, swapping b and d changes I from bd³ to db³; the deflection ratio (inversely proportional to I) works out to (b/d)².

q: 15. The deflection of any rectangular beam simply supported, is
options: inversely proportional to the cube of its depth
directly proportional to the cube of its length
explain: Since deflection δ ∝ 1/I and I ∝ d³ for a rectangular section, deflection is inversely proportional to the cube of the beam's depth.

q: 16. Which of the following section is the most efficient in carrying bending moments?
explain: An I-section is most efficient because most of its area is located in the flanges, far from the neutral axis, providing a high Section Modulus (Z) for a given area.

q: 17. In a continuous bending moment curve the point where its changes sign is called
explain: The point where the bending moment changes sign (from sagging to hogging or vice versa) is known by all these terms in structural engineering.

q: 18. The arch meant for supporting uniformly distributed loads, to avoid any bending moment must be
explain: A parabolic arch is the 'funicular' shape for a uniformly distributed load, meaning it carries the load purely through compression with zero bending moment.

q: 19. The amount of bending moment induced in a cable is
explain: A perfectly flexible cable cannot resist bending; it carries loads through pure tension.

q: 20. The maximum deflection due due to load W at the free end of a cantilever of length L and having flexural rigidity EI is
explain: For a cantilever with a point load W at the free end, the standard maximum tip deflection formula is WL³/3EI.

q: 21. Slope deflection method is
explain: The Slope Deflection method is a displacement (deflection) method of structural analysis that relates end moments to joint rotations and displacements.

q: 22. A simply supported beam is subjected to a pure moment. This will be resisted through
options: a moment reaction at hinged end
a moment reaction at hinge on rollers end
a couple formed by the reaction from the two supports
external support capable of resisting moment which is necessarily to be provided
explain: Since hinge/roller supports cannot resist moment directly, an applied pure moment on a simply supported beam is instead balanced by a couple formed from equal and opposite vertical reactions at the two supports.

q: 23. The assumption that the cross-sections plane before bending remain plane even after bending means
options: the strains in the fibers are proportional to their distances from neutral axis
the bending moment will be resisted by the central core of the section
the stresses in the fibres are proportional to their distances from neutral axis
the neutral axis lies at mid height
explain: Plane sections remaining plane implies a linear variation of strain with distance from the neutral axis, which is the fundamental Bernoulli-Euler bending assumption.

q: 24. The assumption in the theory of bending that the material is homogeneous and isotropic has the same value of Young's Modulus in tension and compression implies that
options: the stresses are proportional to strains at all fibres
the strains are proportional to distances of the fibres from neutral axis
the beam bends into a circular arc
the neutral axis lies at the centre
explain: Equal E in tension and compression (homogeneous, isotropic material) combined with Hooke's law implies stress is proportional to strain uniformly at all fibres of the section.

q: 25. The influence line diagram for S.F. or BM at a section is
options: the value of S.F. or B.M. at that section when the unit load is placed over that section only
the value of S.F. or B.M. at that section when the unit load is at the centre of the span
the variation in the value of S.F. or B.M. at that section as the unit load transverses the span from left to right
explain: An ILD for a section must show the full range of variation (the 'influence') as the unit load moves from the start of the span to the end.

q: 26. The influence line diagram for reaction at the support of a cantilever will be a
options: triangle with zero ordinate at fixed end and unit ordinate at free end
triangle with unit ordinate at fixed end and zero ordinate at free end
explain: In a cantilever, any vertical load placed anywhere on the beam must be fully resisted by the single vertical reaction at the fixed support. Therefore, the reaction is always 1, resulting in a rectangle with unit ordinate.

q: 27. The influence line diagram for shear force at a section on a cantilever will be
options: a rectangle of length equal to full length of span with unit ordinate
a rectangle extending between free end and the section with unit ordinate
a triangle extending for whole length of span with unit ordinate at fixed support
a triangle extending between the section and the fixed end with unit ordinate at fixed support
explain: Shear force at a section in a cantilever only exists when the load is between the free end and that section. If the load is between the fixed support and the section, the shear at that section is zero. This creates a rectangle from the section to the free end.

q: 28. The influence line diagram for BM at a section of a simply supported beam will be a
options: triangle with maximum ordinate at the section and zero at the two supports
triangle with maximum ordinate at the support nearer to the section and zero at the other support
explain: For a simply supported beam, the B.M. at a section 'C' is zero when the load is at either support and reaches its maximum value (ab/L) when the load is directly on the section.

q: 29. Bending moment at A of the following beam is equal to (refer to image 1666)
explain: At a simple end support or hinge, the internal bending moment is zero.

q: 30. The slope and the deflection at a section in a loaded beam cannot be found out by :
explain: Rankine's method is typically used for earth pressure or column buckling, not for determining beam deflection.

q: 31. For a cantilever with a uniformly distributed load of total W over entire length L, the max bending moment is :
explain: If W is the total load ($w \cdot L$), the moment at the fixed end is $W \cdot (L/2) = WL/2$.

q: 32. In approximate analysis of building frames under lateral loads, the point of contraflexure in columns is assumed at
explain: Methods like the Portal and Cantilever methods assume the point of zero moment (contraflexure) is at the mid-height of the column.

q: 33. A beam is a
explain: A beam's length is much larger than its cross-sectional dimensions, classifying it as a one-dimensional structure.

q: 34. The bending moment diagram for a simply supported beam loaded in its centre is
explain: For a simply supported beam with a central point load, the BMD is a symmetric (isosceles) triangle peaking at midspan.

q: 35. A flitched beam is used to
options: change the shape of the beam
equalize the strength in tension and compression
increase the cross-section of the beam
explain: A flitched beam (composite timber-and-steel beam) is used to equalize/balance the strength characteristics in tension and compression by combining materials with complementary properties.

q: 36. The expression EI d⁴y/dx⁴ at any section for a beam is equal to
explain: Differentiating the beam bending equation EI(d²y/dx²)=M twice gives EI(d⁴y/dx⁴) = d²M/dx² = load intensity (since dM/dx=V and dV/dx=-w), so this expression equals the load intensity at the section.

q: 37. The maximum deflection of a simply supported beam of span L, carrying an isolated load at the center of the span
explain: The standard formula for maximum deflection of a simply supported beam under a central point load W is WL³/48EI.

q: 38. Ties are load carrying members of a frame, which are subjected to
explain: A tie is a truss/frame member specifically subjected to axial tension loads.

q: 39. Beams of uniform strength are preferred to those of uniform section because these are economical for
explain: Beams of uniform strength save material by removing unnecessary cross-section where bending moment is low, making them more economical particularly for lighter load applications where material savings matter proportionally more.

q: 40. The moment diagram for a cantilever carrying linearly varying load from zero at its free end and to maximum at the fixed end will be
explain: Integrating a linearly varying (triangular) load twice to get the bending moment produces a cubic variation, giving a cubic parabola moment diagram.
